name: 𐤊𐤍𐤏𐤍
note: Phoenician, the language of Tyre, Sidon and Byblos and of their colonies from Cyprus to Carthage, from the 11th century BC, in its own alphabet of twenty-two letters, right to left: the alphabet the Greek, Latin, Hebrew and Aramaic letters come from. It writes consonants only, so the words are written as the inscriptions write them, without vowels; words are split by spaces rather than the small word divider, so long lines can wrap. Exported Python prints the usual transliteration instead, with ꜣ and ꜥ for aleph and ayin. The inscriptions (dedications, royal building texts, tomb curses, trade) keep a narrow vocabulary, so the sentences follow the Ugaritic file's, its close Northwest Semitic neighbour, respelled for Phoenician's letters and with Phoenician's own grammar words: ʾš for the relative, z for 'this', pʿl for 'make', yš for 'there is', ʾm for 'if', ʾw for 'or', ʾmr for 'say'. Modern ideas are descriptive coinages on attested roots, used the same way everywhere: ʾbn (stone) for block, mknt (what is set up) for program, ntb (path) for script, hlk (going) for run, with lk (go!) on the Run button, ṣlm (image, statue) for model, mlʾk (messenger) for agent, kly (vessel) for tool, bḥn (test) for review, spr rʾš (first writing) for draft, pr (fruit) for result, mšn (what changes) for variable, lḥ (tablet) for file, ʾrn (chest) for folder, mny (counter) for computer, spr ymm (book of days) for calendar, mnt (count) for list, dbr (thing) for record, šd (field) for a record's field, ršt (net) for the web, pnt (face) for page, ṭbʿ (seal impression) for token, mpth (opener) for key, mṣb (standing stone) for checkpoint, ʾgrt (letter) for email and brq (lightning) for electricity. Field names, status values, settings, commands and product names stay as they are, in Latin letters, as in the other languages.
